1928.subject: Zoology
1928.text: Select the option having all the correct characteristics.
1928.sol:
Options (a), (b), (c) and (d) show neutrophil, basophil, eosinophil and monocyte respectively. Neutrophils are the most abundant cells (60-65\%) of the total WBCs and basophils are the least (0.5 - $1 \%)$ among them. Neutrophils and monocytes $(6-8 \%)$ are phagocytic cells. Which destroy foreign organisms entering the body.
Basophils secrete histamine, serotonin, heparin, etc. and are involved in inflammatory reactions. Eosinophils (2 - 3\%) resist infections and are also associated with allergic reactions.

4715.text: The pair of xenon compounds, which have a& same number of lone pairs of electrons on the central atom is
4715.sol:
$\left(1\right){XeO}_{3}$:~Xenon contains& $8$~electrons in its valence shell,& $6$~electrons& are used in bonding with three oxygen atoms& and $2$ electrons~remain unbonded,& i.e.,& $1$~lone pair of electrons.

$\left(2\right){XeF}_{6}$:~Xenon contains& $8$~electrons in its valence shell,& $6$~electrons& are used in bonding with six fluorine atoms& and& $2$ electrons~remain unbonded, i.e.,& $1$~lone pair of electrons.

$\left(3\right){XeF}_{2}$:~Xenon contains& $8$~electrons in its valence shell,& $2$~electrons& are used in bonding with two fluorine atoms& and& $6$~electrons remain unbonded, i.e.,& $3$~lone pairs of electrons.

$\left(4\right){XeF}_{4}$:~Xenon contains& $8$~electrons in its valence shell,& $4$~electrons are used in bonding with four fluorine atoms& and& $4$~electrons remain unbonded, i.e.,& $2$~lone pairs of electrons.

$\left(5\right){XeOF}_{4}$:~Xenon contains& $8$~electrons in its valence shell,& $4$~electrons& are used in bonding with four fluorine atoms and& $2$ electrons~are used in bonding with one oxygen atom and $2$ electrons remain unbonded, i.e.,~$1$~lone pair of electrons.

Hence, the pair of xenon compounds, which have a same number of lone pairs of electrons on the central atom is& ${XeO}_{3}$~and& ${XeF}_{6}$.

7827.subject: Mathematics
7827.sol:
Let

$I = {∫}_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{xtanx}{secx + tanx}dx$

$= {∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left\{\dfrac{\left(\pi - x\right)tan\left(\pi - x\right)}{sec\left(\pi - x\right) + tan\left(\pi - x\right)}\right\}dx$

$= {∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left\{\dfrac{\left(\pi - x\right)\left(- tanx\right)}{- secx - tanx}\right\}dx$

$= {∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left\{\dfrac{\left(\pi - x\right)\left(\tan x\right)}{secx + tanx}\right\}dx$

$= {∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left\{\dfrac{\pi\left(\tan x\right)}{secx + tanx}\right\}dx - {∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left\{\dfrac{x\left(\tan x\right)}{secx + tanx}\right\}dx$

$= {∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left\{\dfrac{\pi\left(\tan x\right)}{secx + tanx}\right\}dx - I$

$⇒ 2I = \pi{∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left\{\dfrac{tanx}{secx + tanx}\right\}dx$

$⇒ 2I = \pi{∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left\{\left(\dfrac{sinx}{cosx}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{cosx}\right) + \left(\dfrac{sinx}{cosx}\right)\right\}dx$

$⇒ 2I = \pi{∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left\{\dfrac{sinx}{1 + sinx}\right\}dx$

$⇒ 2I = \pi{∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left\{sinx\left(1 - sinx\right)\left(1 - \sin^{2}x\right)\right\}dx$

$⇒ 2I = \pi{∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left\{\dfrac{sinx}{\cos^{2}x} - \dfrac{\sin^{2}x}{\cos^{2}x}\right\}dx$

$⇒ 2I = \pi{∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left(tanxsecx - \tan^{2}x\right)dx$

$⇒ 2I = \pi{secx - tanx + x}_{0}^{\pi}$

$⇒ 2I = \pi \left[ \left(sec \pi -$ tan $\pi + \pi\right) - \left(sec0 - tan0 + 0\right)\right]$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{\pi\left(\pi - 2\right)}{2}.$

Also, $\mathrm{u} \mu \mathrm{T}\begin{aligned} & \therefore \frac{\mathrm{H}}{\mathrm{ T}} \propto \mathrm{ T} \Rightarrow \mathrm{H} \propto \mathrm{ T}^2 \Rightarrow\left(\frac{\mathrm{ T}_2}{\mathrm{ T}_1}\right)=\sqrt{\frac{1.1 \mathrm{H}_1}{\mathrm{H}_1}}=\sqrt{1.1} \\ & \therefore \mathrm{ T}_2=\sqrt{1.1} \mathrm{ T}_1=1.05 \mathrm{ T}_1 \\ & \therefore \Delta \mathrm{ T} \%=5 \% \end{aligned}$

18482.text: For two events A and B , if $\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A})=\mathrm{P}\left(\frac{\mathrm{A}}{\mathrm{B}}\right)=\frac{1}{4}$ and $P\left(\frac{B}{A}\right)=\frac{1}{2}$, then which of the following is not true?
18482.sol:
$\mathrm{P}\left(\frac{\mathrm{B}}{\mathrm{A}}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{B} \cap \mathrm{A})}{\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A})}=\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{B} \cap \mathrm{A})=\frac{1}{8}\mathrm{P}\left(\frac{\mathrm{A}}{\mathrm{B}}\right)=\frac{1}{4} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A} \cap \mathrm{B})}{\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{B})}=\frac{1}{4} \Rightarrow \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{B})=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A} \cap \mathrm{B})=\frac{1}{8}=\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A}) \cdot \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{B})\therefore$ Events A and B are independent.
Now, $\mathrm{P}\left(\frac{\mathrm{A}^{\prime}}{\mathrm{B}}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A} \cap \mathrm{B})}{\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{B})}=\frac{\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A}) \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{B})}{\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{B})}=\frac{3}{4}$
and $\mathrm{P}\left(\frac{\mathrm{B}^{\prime}}{\mathrm{A}^{\prime}}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{B}^{\prime} \cap \mathrm{A}^{\prime}\right)}{\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{A}^{\prime}\right)}=\frac{\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{B}^{\prime}\right) \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{A}^{\prime}\right)}{\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{A}^{\prime}\right)}=\frac{1}{2}$

Match the compounds given in column I with the corresponding most stable Carbocations formed by each, as given in Column II, when they undergo acidic dehydration in presence of Conc. $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4$.
No.Column INo.Column II
A2-Methylbu\tan^{-1}-olP$(CH_3)_2\overset{+}{C} - CH(CH_3)_2$
BButan-2-olQ$CH_3 - CH_2 - CH_2 - \overset{+}{C}H_2$

For 2-Methylbu\tan^{-1}-ol (A): The initial carbocation is $CH_3CH_2CH(CH_3)CH_2^{+}$. A 1,2-hydride shift occurs to form the more stable tertiary carbocation $(CH_3)_2C^{+}CH_2CH_3$, which corresponds to R.

20945.subject: Mathematics
20945.text: $\text{ The function } f(x)=\tan ^{-1}(\sin x+\cos x) \text{$ is an increasing function in }
20945.sol:
Given $f(x) = \tan^{-1}(\sin x + \cos x)$.

To determine the interval where $f(x)$ is increasing, we find the derivative $f'(x)$ and set $f'(x) \gt 0$.

$f'(x) = \dfrac{1}{1 + (\sin x + \cos x)^2} \cdot \dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x + \cos x)$

$f'(x) = \dfrac{\cos x - \sin x}{1 + (\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x + 2 \sin x \cos x)}$

$f'(x) = \dfrac{\cos x - \sin x}{1 + 1 + \sin(2x)} = \dfrac{\cos x - \sin x}{2 + \sin(2x)}$

Since the denominator $2 + \sin(2x)$ is always positive for all real $x$, the sign of $f'(x)$ depends only on the numerator $\cos x - \sin x$.

For $f(x)$ to be increasing, we require $f'(x) \gt 0$, which implies $\cos x - \sin x \gt 0$.

$\cos x \gt \sin x$

Dividing by $\cos x$ (assuming $\cos x \gt 0$, which holds in the interval $(-\pi/2, \pi/2)$):

$1 \gt \tan x$

$\tan x \lt 1$

In the interval $(-\pi/2, \pi/2)$, $\tan x \lt 1$ holds when $x \lt \pi/4$.

Thus, the function is increasing in the interval $(-\pi/2, \pi/4)$.

Answer: $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$

21166.subject: Mathematics
21166.text: Given that $z$ is a real number and $z=\dfrac{\lambda+4 i}{1+\lambda i}$ where $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then the possible value of $\lambda$ is
21166.sol:
Given $z = \dfrac{\lambda + 4i}{1 + \lambda i}$, where $z \in R$.

To ensure $z$ is real, the imaginary part of $z$ must be zero. Multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, $1 - \lambda i$:

$z = \dfrac{(\lambda + 4i)(1 - \lambda i)}{(1 + \lambda i)(1 - \lambda i)}$

$z = \dfrac{\lambda - \lambda^2 i + 4i - 4\lambda i^2}{1^2 + \lambda^2}$

Since $i^2 = -1$, we have:

$z = \dfrac{\lambda + 4\lambda i + (4 - \lambda^2)i}{1 + \lambda^2} = \dfrac{\lambda}{1 + \lambda^2} + i \dfrac{4 - \lambda^2}{1 + \lambda^2}$

For $z$ to be real, the imaginary part must be zero:

$\dfrac{4 - \lambda^2}{1 + \lambda^2} = 0$

$4 - \lambda^2 = 0$

$\lambda^2 = 4$

$\lambda = \pm 2$.

Checking the options provided, $-2$ is a valid value for $\lambda$.

Answer: $-2$

21529.text: The area of the region bounded by the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ is
21529.sol:
The equation of the ellipse is $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$.

Solving for $y$, we get $y = \pm \dfrac{b}{a} \sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$.

The area $A$ of the ellipse is given by $4 \times \int_{0}^{a} y \, dx = 4 \int_{0}^{a} \dfrac{b}{a} \sqrt{a^2 - x^2} \, dx$.

$A = \dfrac{4b}{a} \int_{0}^{a} \sqrt{a^2 - x^2} \, dx$.

Using the standard integral $\int \sqrt{a^2 - x^2} \, dx = \dfrac{x}{2} \sqrt{a^2 - x^2} + \dfrac{a^2}{2} \sin^{-1} \left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right), we evaluate the definite integral:

$ A = $\dfrac{4b}{a} \left[ \dfrac{x}{2} \sqrt{a^2 - x^2} + \dfrac{a^2}{2} \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right) \right]_{0}^{a}.

$ A = $\dfrac{4b}{a} \left(0 + \dfrac{a^2}{2} \sin^{-1}(1) - (0 + 0) \right) = \dfrac{4b}{a} \times \dfrac{a^2}{2} \times \dfrac{\pi}{2}.

$ A = $\pi$ a b$.

Answer: \pi$ a b$ sq units$

21548.sol:
The integral is given by $I = \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{9+8x-x^2}} dx$.

Complete the square for the quadratic expression inside the square root:
$9 + 8x - x^2 = 9 - (x^2 - 8x) = 9 - (x^2 - 8x + 16 - 16) = 9 - ((x-4)^2 - 16) = 9 + 16 - (x-4)^2 = 25 - (x-4)^2$.

Substitute this into the integral:
$I = \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{25 - (x-4)^2}} dx$.

Using the standard integral formula $\int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a^2 - u^2}} du = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{u}{a}\right) + C$, where $a = 5$ and $u = x-4$, we get:
$I = \sin^{-1} \left(\dfrac{x-4}{5}\right) +$C$.

Thus, \varphi(x) = \sin^{-1} $\$left(\dfrac{x-4}{5}\right).$

Answer: \sin ^{-1} \$left(\dfrac{x-4}{5}\right)$

21574.subject: Mathematics
21574.sol:
Let $I = \int \dfrac{3^x}{\sqrt{1-9^x}} dx$.

Rewrite the denominator as $\sqrt{1-(3^x)^2}$.

Let $u = 3^x$. Then $du = 3^x \ln 3 dx$, which implies $3^x dx = \dfrac{du}{\ln 3}$.

Substituting these into the integral:

$I = \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}} \cdot \dfrac{du}{\ln 3}$

$I = \dfrac{1}{\ln 3} \int \dfrac{du}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}$

Using the standard integral formula $\int \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = \sin^{-1} x + C$, we get:

$I = \dfrac{1}{\ln 3} \sin^{-1} u + C$

Substituting $u = 3^x$ back:

$I = \dfrac{1}{\ln 3} \sin^{-1} 3^x + C$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{\log 3} \sin ^{-1} 3^x+C$

22359.subject: Physics
22359.text: A series LCR circuit is connected to an AC source of 120 V and 60 Hz . The value of resistance R in the circuit is $100 \Omega$.A voltmeter reads the voltage across R as 50 V , across the inductor as 132 V and across the capacitor as $\dfrac{70}{6.6} \mathrm{ V}$. The value of inductance and capacitance in the circuit is:
22359.sol:
Given $V_{R} = 50 \text{ V}$, $V_{L} = 132 \text{ V}$, $V_{C} = \dfrac{70}{6.6} \text{ V} \approx 10.6 \text{ V}$, and $R = 100 \Omega$.

The current in the series LCR circuit is $I = \dfrac{V_{R}}{R} = \dfrac{50}{100} = 0.5 \text{ A}$.

The inductive reactance $X_{L}$ is given by $X_{L} = \dfrac{V_{L}}{I} = \dfrac{132}{0.5} = 264 \Omega$.

Since $X_{L} = 2\pi f L$, where $f = 60 \text{ Hz}$, we have $L = \dfrac{264}{2 \times \pi \times 60} = \dfrac{264}{377} \approx 0.7 \text{ H}$.

The capacitive reactance $X_{C}$ is given by $X_{C} = \dfrac{V_{C}}{I} = \dfrac{70 / 6.6}{0.5} = \dfrac{140}{6.6} \approx 21.21 \Omega$.

Since $X_{C} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi f C}$, we have $C = \dfrac{1}{2 \times \pi \times 60 \times (140 / 6.6)} = \dfrac{6.6}{2 \times \pi \times 60 \times 140} = \dfrac{6.6}{52778} \approx 1.25 \times 10^{-4} \text{ F} = 125 \mu \text{F}$.

Comparing these values with the options, the inductance is $0.7 \text{ H}$ and the capacitance is $125 \mu \text{F}$.

Answer: 0.7 H and $125 \mu \mathrm{ F}$

22572.subject: Physics
22572.text: In the figure shown above, a cell of negligible internal resistance and emf 22 V is connected to a network of resistors. If the power dissipated in the whole circuit is $\dfrac{x}{10 R}$, then the value of $x$ is:
22572.sol:
The diamond network forms a Wheatstone bridge. Left arm ratio: $\dfrac{4R}{8R} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, Right arm ratio: $\dfrac{2R}{4R} = \dfrac{1}{2}$. Since ratios are equal, the bridge is balanced — no current flows through the horizontal branch ($R + R = 2R$), so it is removed.

Remaining three parallel paths in the diamond:
Left path: $4R + 8R = 12R$
Right path: $2R + 4R = 6R$
Vertical path: $R + R = 2R$

Combining left and right paths in parallel:
$R_{outer} = \dfrac{12R \times 6R}{12R + 6R} = \dfrac{72R^2}{18R} = 4R$

Combining with vertical path:
$R_{diamond} = \dfrac{4R \times 2R}{4R + 2R} = \dfrac{8R^2}{6R} = \dfrac{4}{3}R$

Total resistance (including top $R$ and bottom $R$ in series):
$R_{total} = R + \dfrac{4}{3}R + R = \dfrac{10}{3}R$

Total power: $P = \dfrac{V^2}{R_{total}} = \dfrac{(22)^2}{\dfrac{10}{3}R} = \dfrac{484 \times 3}{10R} = \dfrac{1452}{10R}$

Comparing with $\dfrac{x}{10R}$: $x = 1452$

23340.subject: Physics
23340.text: An object is placed at an unknown distance from a convex objective lens of focal length 8 cm. The objective lens forms a real image which acts as an object for a convex eyepiece of focal length 6.25 cm. The distance between the objective and eyepiece is 45 cm. The microscope is adjusted so that the final image is formed at the least distance of distinct vision (25 cm). Which of the following is correct?
23340.sol:
For the eyepiece, the final image is formed at the least distance of distinct vision, so $v_e = -25 \text{ cm}$.

Using the lens formula for the eyepiece:

$\dfrac{1}{v_e} - \dfrac{1}{u_e} = \dfrac{1}{f_e}$

$\dfrac{1}{-25} - \dfrac{1}{u_e} = \dfrac{1}{6.25}$

$-\dfrac{1}{u_e} = \dfrac{1}{6.25} + \dfrac{1}{25} = \dfrac{4}{25} + \dfrac{1}{25} = \dfrac{5}{25} = \dfrac{1}{5}$

$u_e = -5 \text{ cm}$

The distance between the objective and the eyepiece is $L = v_o + |u_e|$, where $v_o$ is the image distance for the objective lens.

$45 = v_o + |-5|$

$v_o = 45 - 5 = 40 \text{ cm}$

Using the lens formula for the objective lens:

$\dfrac{1}{v_o} - \dfrac{1}{u_o} = \dfrac{1}{f_o}$

$\dfrac{1}{40} - \dfrac{1}{u_o} = \dfrac{1}{8}$

$-\dfrac{1}{u_o} = \dfrac{1}{8} - \dfrac{1}{40} = \dfrac{5 - 1}{40} = \dfrac{4}{40} = \dfrac{1}{10}$

$u_o = -10 \text{ cm}$

The object distance is $10 \text{ cm}$.

The total magnification $m$ of the microscope is the product of the linear magnifications of the objective and the eyepiece.

$m = m_o \times m_e = \left(\dfrac{v_o}{u_o}\right) \times\left(\dfrac{v_e}{u_e}\right)

$m = $\left(\dfrac{40}{-10}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{-25}{-5}\right) = (-4) \times5 = -20$

The magnitude of the total magnification is $20$.

If the jar is kept at temperature $T$, what is the ratio of the total pressure of the combined gas to the partial pressure due to the gas $A$?
24307.sol:
Let $m_A$ and $m_B$ be the molar masses of gases $A$ and $B$ respectively.

Given $m_A = 2m_B$.

Number of moles of gas $A$, $n_A = \dfrac{M_A}{m_A}$

Number of moles of gas $B$, $n_B = \dfrac{M_B}{m_B}$

According to Dalton's law of partial pressures, the partial pressure of a gas is proportional to its number of moles.

Partial pressure of $A$, $P_A = \dfrac{n_A RT}{V}$

Total pressure, $P = \dfrac{(n_A + n_B) RT}{V}$

The ratio of the total pressure to the partial pressure of $A$ is:

$\dfrac{P}{P_A} = \dfrac{n_A + n_B}{n_A} = 1 + \dfrac{n_B}{n_A}$

Substituting the values of $n_A$ and $n_B$:

$\dfrac{P}{P_A} = 1 + \dfrac{\dfrac{M_B}{m_B}}{\dfrac{M_A}{m_A}} = 1 + \dfrac{M_B}{M_A} \times \dfrac{m_A}{m_B}$

Since $m_A = 2m_B$, we get $\dfrac{m_A}{m_B} = 2$.

$\dfrac{P}{P_A} = 1 + 2\dfrac{M_B}{M_A}$

Answer: $1 + 2\dfrac{M_B}{M_A}$

$( A )$ In ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$ , if the magnitude of the projection vector of the vector $\alpha\overset{^}{i} + \beta\overset{^}{j}$ on $\sqrt{3}\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j}$ is $\sqrt{3}$ and if $\alpha = 2 + \sqrt{3}\beta,$ then possible value (s) of $| \alpha |$ is (are) $\left(P\right)$ 1

$( C )$ Let $\omega \ne 1$ be a complex cube roots of unity. If ${\left(3 - 3\omega + 2{\omega}^{2}\right)}^{4n + 3} + {\left(2 + 3\omega - 3{\omega}^{2}\right)}^{4n + 3} + {\left(- 3 + 2\omega + 3{\omega}^{2}\right)}^{4n + 3} = 0$ then possible value (s) of n is (are) $\left(R\right)$ 3

$- 3a - 2 = - 6a + {a}^{2}$

$⇒ {\left(3 - 3\omega + 2{\omega}^{2}\right)}^{4n + 3}\left\{1 + {\omega}^{4n} + {\omega}^{8n}\right\} = 0$
So, $n = 1, 2, 4, 5$

Let $q - q = \alpha, d = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}$
$a = 5 - \dfrac{\alpha}{2}, b = a + \dfrac{3\alpha}{2} = 5 + \alpha$
Now, $\dfrac{ab}{a + b} = 2$
$⇒ \dfrac{\left(5 - \dfrac{\alpha}{2}\right)\left(5 + \alpha\right)}{5 - \dfrac{\alpha}{2} + 5 + \alpha} = 2$

26182.text:
A positive point charge of $10^{-8} \mathrm{C}$ is kept at a distance of 20 cm from the center of a neutral conducting sphere of radius 10 cm . The sphere is then grounded and the charge on the sphere is measured. The grounding is then removed and subsequently the point charge is moved by a distance of 10 cm further away from the center of the sphere along the radial direction. Taking $\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0}=9 \times 10^9 \mathrm{Nm}^2 / \mathrm{C}^2$ (where $\epsilon_0$ is the permittivity of free space), which of the following
statements is/are correct: :
options: Before the grounding, the electrostatic potential of the sphere is 450 V .
Charge flowing from the sphere to the ground because of grounding is $5 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{C}$.
After the grounding is removed, the charge on the sphere is $-5 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{C}$.
The final electrostatic potential of the sphere is 300 V .

Before grounding
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{V}_{\text{sphere }}=\left(\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{C}}\right)_{\text{net }}=\left(\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{C}}\right)_{\mathrm{q}}+\left(\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{C}}\right)_{\text{ind }} \\ & \mathrm{V}_{\text{sphere }}=\frac{\mathrm{kq}}{\ell}+0=\frac{9 \times 10^9 \times 10^{-8}}{0.2}=\frac{90}{0.2}=\frac{900}{2}=450 \mathrm{volt}\end{aligned}$
After grounding$\begin{aligned} & \frac{\mathrm{kQ}}{\ell}+\frac{\mathrm{kq}_{\mathrm{S}}}{\mathrm{R}}=\mathrm{V}_{\text{sphere }^{\prime}=0 \\ & \mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{s}}=-\frac{\mathrm{R}}{\ell} \mathrm{q}=-\frac{1}{2} \times 10^{-8}=-5 \times 10^{-9} \\ & \mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{s}}=-5 \times 10^{-9} \text{ Coulomb }\end{aligned}$
Charge flower from sphere to ground $=5 \times 10^{-9}$ Coulomb
After grounding is removed
$\begin{aligned} & \left(\mathrm{V}_{\text{sphere }}\right)_{\text{final }}=\frac{\mathrm{kq}}{\ell^{\prime}}+\frac{\mathrm{kq}_{\mathrm{s}}}{\mathrm{R}} \\ & =\frac{9 \times 10^9 \times 10^2 \times 10^{-8}}{30}-\frac{9 \times 10^9 \times 5 \times 10^{-9} \times 10^2}{10} \\ & =\frac{9 \times 1000}{30}-450=300 \mathrm{volt}-450 \mathrm{volt}=-150 \mathrm{volt}\end{aligned}$

26640.text:
A current carrying wire heats a metal rod. The wire provides a constant power $\left(P\right)$ to the rod. The metal rod is enclosed in an insulated container. It is observed that the temperature $\left(T\right)$ in the metal rod changes with time $\left(t\right)$ as:
$T\left(t\right)$ = {T}_{0}$\left(1 + \beta{t}^{1 / 4}\right)$
where $\beta$ is a constant with appropriate dimension while ${T}_{0}$ is a constant with dimension of temperature. The heat capacity of the metal is:
26640.sol:
Heat required for small increment in temperature of a substance is given by
$dQ = m . s . dT$
where, $m =$ mass of substances
or $s =$ specific heat of substance
Now, heat capacity, $H = m . s .$
$∴ dQ = H . dT$
$⇒$ Rate of heat absorption by the rod, $\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = P = H ⋅ \dfrac{dT}{dt}$ .......(1)
But given that, temperature of rod as a function of time is
$T = {T}_{0}\left(1 + \beta{t}^{1 / 4}\right)$ ......(2)
$⇒ \dfrac{dT}{dt} = {T}_{0} ⋅ \beta ⋅ \dfrac{1}{4}{t}^{- \dfrac{3}{4}}$
Putting it in (1) gives
$P = H ⋅ {T}_{0} ⋅ \beta ⋅ \dfrac{1}{4} ⋅ {t}^{- \dfrac{3}{4}}$
$⇒ H = \dfrac{4P ⋅ {t}^{3 / 4}}{{T}_{0} ⋅ \beta}$
$⇒ H = 4P\dfrac{{\left(T - {T}_{0}\right)}^{3}}{{T}_{0}^{4} ⋅ {B}^{4}}$
Now using equation $( 2 )$
$T - {T}_{0} = {T}_{0}\beta ⋅ {t}^{1 / 4}$
$⇒ {t}^{3 / 4} = {T}_{0}{\left(\dfrac{T - {T}_{0}}{{T}_{0}\beta}\right)}^{3}$

28673.text: Total number of unpaired electrons present in the central metal atoms/ions of $\left[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{CO})_{4}\right],\left[\mathrm{NiCl}_{4}\right]^{2-},\left[\mathrm{PtCl}_{2}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{2}\right],\left[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{CN})_{4}\right]^{2-}$ and $\left[\mathrm{Pt}(\mathrm{CN})_{4}\right]^{2-}$ is $\_\_\_\_$.
28673.sol:
$[Ni(CO)_4]$:
Ni is zero-valent with configuration $[Ar]3d^{10}4s^2$.
CO is a strong field ligand causing complete pairing in the filled $3d^{10}$ orbital.
Unpaired electrons = 0.

$[NiCl_4]^{2-}$:
Ni is $+2$ with configuration $[Ar]3d^8$.
Cl is a weak field ligand producing high-spin tetrahedral geometry with configuration $3d^8$: five orbitals with two electrons paired, three electrons unpaired.
Unpaired electrons = 2.

$[PtCl_2(NH_3)_2]$:
Pt is $+2$ with configuration $[Xe]4f^{14}5d^8$.
Pt(II) adopts square planar geometry with strong-field splitting leading to complete pairing: $5d^8$ configuration places all electrons in bonding orbitals.
Unpaired electrons = 0.

$[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$:
Ni is $+2$ with $3d^8$ configuration.
CN is a strong field ligand.
Square planar geometry is preferred, resulting in all electrons paired.
Unpaired electrons = 0.

$[Pt(CN)_4]^{2-}$:
Pt is $+2$ with $5d^8$ configuration.
CN is a strong field ligand producing square planar geometry with complete pairing.
Unpaired electrons = 0.

Total unpaired electrons = 0 + 2 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 2.

29761.subject: Chemistry
29761.text: A species having carbon with sextet of electrons and can act as electrophile is called
29761.sol:
A carbocation is a molecule in which a carbon atom has a positive charge and three bonds. We can say that, basically, they are carbon cations. Formerly, it was known as carbonium ion. Carbocation today is defined as any even-electron cation that possesses a significant positive charge on the carbon atom.

The carbon cations are very reactive and unstable due to an incomplete octet. In simple words, carbocations do not have eight electrons; therefore, they do not satisfy the octet rule.

In carbocation, the hybridisation of carbon will be ${sp}^{2}$ and its shape is trigonal planar. There is also a vacant $p -$ orbital which indicates its electron-deficient nature. The carbon has $6$ electrons in its valence shell. Due to this, it is an electron-deficient species, also known as an electrophile.

29766.subject: Chemistry
29766.text: Which among the following purification methods is based on the principle of “Solubility” in two different solvents?
29766.sol:
In chemistry, differential extraction is defined as a technique that is used to separate any organic compound that is present in an aqueous solution from the rest of the solution. The process of liquid-liquid extraction is the most commonly used in the chemistry laboratory, and it takes place in a separatory funnel.

The organic compound is later recovered by the process of distillation or evaporation. The process of continuous extraction is used in cases when the solubility of the compound is less in the organic solvent.

32853.subject: Mathematics
32853.text: If the equation of the normal to the curve $y = \dfrac{x - a}{\left(x + b\right)\left(x - 2\right)}$ at the point $\left(1, - 3\right)$ is $x - 4y = 13$ then the value of $a + b$ is equal to ______
32853.sol:
Given curve is

$y = \dfrac{x - a}{\left(x + b\right)\left(x - 2\right)} . . . \left(1\right)$

At point $\left(1, - 3\right)$, we have

$- 3 = \dfrac{1 - a}{\left(1 + b\right)\left(1 - 2\right)}$

$⇒ 3\left(1 + b\right) = 1 - a$

$⇒ 1 - a = 3 + 3b$

Differentiating $\left(1\right)$ both sides w.r.t. $x$, we get

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{( x + b ) ( x - 2 ) \times ( 1 ) - ( x - a ) ( 2x + b - 2 )}{( x + b{)}^{2} ( x - 2{)}^{2}}$

At $( 1, - 3 )$ slope of normal is $\dfrac{1}{4}$, hence

$\dfrac{dx}{dy} = - \dfrac{1}{4}$

$⇒ {\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}_{\left(1, - 3\right)} = - 4$,

$⇒ - 4 = \dfrac{( 1 + b ) ( - 1 ) - ( 1 - a ) b}{( 1 + b{)}^{2} ( - 1{)}^{2}}$

$⇒ - 4 = \dfrac{( 1 + b ) ( - 1 ) - 3 ( b + 1 ) b}{( 1 + b{)}^{2}}$

$⇒ - 4 = \dfrac{\left(- 1\right) - 3b}{\left(1 + b\right)}$

$\left[∵ b \ne - 1\right]$

$⇒ 4 + 4b = 1 + 3b$

$⇒ b = - 3$

So, $a = 7$

Hence, $a + b = 4$

If $b$ is very small as compared to the value of $a$, so that the cube and other higher powers of $\dfrac{b}{a}$ can be neglected in the identity

$\dfrac{1}{a - b} + \dfrac{1}{a - 2b} + \dfrac{1}{a - 3b} + \ldots . + \dfrac{1}{a - nb} = \alphan + \beta{n}^{2} + \gamma{n}^{3}$

then the value of $\gamma$ is :

Given,

$\dfrac{1}{a - b} + \dfrac{1}{a - 2b} + \dfrac{1}{a - 3b} + \ldots . + \dfrac{1}{a - nb}$

$= {\left(a - b\right)}^{- 1} + {\left(a - 2b\right)}^{- 1} + \ldots . + {\left(a - nb\right)}^{- 1}$

$= \dfrac{1}{a}\mathop{∑}_{r = 1}^{n}{\left(1 - \dfrac{rb}{a}\right)}^{- 1}$

$= \dfrac{1}{a}\mathop{∑}_{r = 1}^{n}\left\{\left(1 + \dfrac{rb}{a} + \dfrac{{r}^{2}{b}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}\right) + \left(termstobeneglected\right)\right\}$

$= \dfrac{1}{a}\left[n + \dfrac{n ( n + 1 )}{2} \cdot \dfrac{b}{a} + \dfrac{n ( n + 1 ) ( 2n + 1 )}{6} \cdot \dfrac{{b}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}\right]$

$= \dfrac{1}{a}\left[n + \dfrac{{n}^{2} + n}{2} \cdot \dfrac{b}{a} + \dfrac{2{n}^{3} + 3{n}^{2} + n}{6} \cdot \dfrac{{b}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}\right]$

So $\gamma = \dfrac{{b}^{2}}{3{a}^{3}}$

33752.subject: Mathematics
33752.text: Let $x$ and $y$ be real numbers such that $50\left(\dfrac{2x}{1+3i} - \dfrac{y}{1-2i}\right) = 31 + 17i$, $i = \sqrt{-1}$. Then the value of $10(x - 3y)$ is :
33752.sol:
Given the equation:

$50\left(\dfrac{2x}{1+3i} - \dfrac{y}{1-2i}\right) = 31 + 17i$

Rationalizing the denominators inside the parentheses:

$\dfrac{2x}{1+3i} = \dfrac{2x(1-3i)}{(1+3i)(1-3i)} = \dfrac{2x(1-3i)}{1^2 + 3^2} = \dfrac{2x(1-3i)}{10} = \dfrac{x(1-3i)}{5}$

$\dfrac{y}{1-2i} = \dfrac{y(1+2i)}{(1-2i)(1+2i)} = \dfrac{y(1+2i)}{1^2 + 2^2} = \dfrac{y(1+2i)}{5}$

Substituting these back into the given equation:

$50\left(\dfrac{x(1-3i)}{5} - \dfrac{y(1+2i)}{5}\right) = 31 + 17i$

$10(x(1-3i) - y(1+2i)) = 31 + 17i$

$10(x - y) - 10i(3x + 2y) = 31 + 17i$

Equating the real and imaginary parts on both sides:

$10(x - y) = 31 \Rightarrow 10x - 10y = 31$

$-10(3x + 2y) = 17 \Rightarrow -30x - 20y = 17$

Multiplying the first equation by $3$ gives:

$30x - 30y = 93$

Adding this to the second equation:

$(-30x - 20y) + (30x - 30y) = 17 + 93$

$-50y = 110 \Rightarrow y = -\dfrac{11}{5}$

Substituting $y = -\dfrac{11}{5}$ into $10x - 10y = 31$:

$10x - 10\left(-\dfrac{11}{5}\right) = 31$

$10x + 22 = 31 \Rightarrow 10x = 9 \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{9}{10}$

Now, finding the value of $10(x - 3y)$:

$10(x - 3y) = 10x - 30y = 10\left(\dfrac{9}{10}\right) - 30\left(-\dfrac{11}{5}\right)$

$10(x - 3y) = 9 + 66 = 75$

Answer: $75$

33896.text: Let $\alpha = \dfrac{- 1 + i\sqrt{3}}{2}$. If $a = \left(1 + \alpha\right)\mathop{∑}_{k = 0}^{100}{\alpha}^{2k}$ and $b = \mathop{∑}_{k = 0}^{100}{\alpha}^{3k}$, then $a$ and $b$, are the roots of the quadratic equation.
33896.sol:
Given,

$\alpha = \dfrac{- 1 + i\sqrt{3}}{2}$

$a = \left(1 + \alpha\right)\mathop{∑}_{k = 0}^{100}{\alpha}^{2k}$ and

$b = \mathop{∑}_{k = 0}^{100}{\alpha}^{3k}$

Now

$\alpha = \omega; \omega = \dfrac{- 1 + i\sqrt{3}}{2}$

Using this $a$ and $b$ can be written as
$a = \left(1 + \omega\right)\left(1 + {\omega}^{2} + {\omega}^{4} + \ldots {\omega}^{198} + {\omega}^{200}\right)$
$= \left(1 + \omega\right)\dfrac{\left(1 - {\left({\omega}^{2}\right)}^{101}\right)}{1 - {\omega}^{2}} = \dfrac{\left(1 + \omega\right)\left(1 - \omega\right)}{1 - {\omega}^{2}} = 1$

Similarly,

$b = 1 + {\omega}^{3} + {\omega}^{6} + \ldots + {\omega}^{300} = 101$
So, the required quadratic equation is

${x}^{2} - \left(a + b\right)x + ab = 0$

$⇒ {x}^{2} - 102x + 101 = 0$.

34434.subject: Mathematics
34434.text:
The sum of all possible values of $\theta \in [0, 2\pi]$, for which the system of equations :
$x\cos 3\theta - 8y - 12z = 0$
$x\cos 2\theta + 3y + 3z = 0$
$x + y + 3z = 0$
has a non-trivial solution, is equal to :
34434.sol:
For the given system of homogeneous linear equations to have a non-trivial solution, the determinant of the coefficient matrix must be zero.

$\begin{vmatrix} \cos 3\theta & -8 & -12 \\ \cos 2\theta & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding the determinant along the first row:

$\cos 3\theta (9 - 3) - (-8)(3\cos 2\theta - 3) + (-12)(\cos 2\theta - 3) = 0$

$6\cos 3\theta + 24\cos 2\theta - 24 - 12\cos 2\theta + 36 = 0$

$6\cos 3\theta + 12\cos 2\theta + 12 = 0$

Dividing by $6$, we get:

$\cos 3\theta + 2\cos 2\theta + 2 = 0$

Using the multiple angle formulas $\cos 3\theta = 4\cos^3 \theta - 3\cos \theta$ and $\cos 2\theta = 2\cos^2 \theta - 1$, we substitute these into the equation:

$(4\cos^3 \theta - 3\cos \theta) + 2(2\cos^2 \theta - 1) + 2 = 0$

$4\cos^3 \theta + 4\cos^2 \theta - 3\cos \theta = 0$

$\cos \theta (4\cos^2 \theta + 4\cos \theta - 3) = 0$

$\cos \theta (2\cos \theta - 1)(2\cos \theta + 3) = 0$

This gives the possible values for $\cos \theta$:

$\cos \theta = 0 \implies \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$

$\cos \theta = \dfrac{1}{2} \implies \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$

$\cos \theta = -\dfrac{3}{2}$ (Not possible since $\cos \theta \in [-1, 1]$)

The possible values of $\theta \in [0, 2\pi]$ are $\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$.

Sum of all possible values of $\theta$:

$\sum \theta = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} + \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) + \left(\dfrac{\pi}{3} + \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\right) = 2\pi + 2\pi = 4\pi$

Answer: $4\pi$

37023.text: Let $a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots$ be an A.P. and $g_1 = a_1, g_2, g_3, \ldots$ be an increasing G.P. If $a_1 = a_2 + g_2 = 1$ and $a_3 + g_3 = 4$, then $a_{10} + g_5$ is equal to:
37023.sol:
Let the common difference of the A.P. be $d$ and the common ratio of the G.P. be $r$.

Given $a_1 = 1$ and $g_1 = a_1 = 1$.

From $a_2 + g_2 = 1$, we have:
$(a_1 + d) + g_1 r = 1$
$1 + d + r = 1 \Rightarrow d = -r$

From $a_3 + g_3 = 4$, we have:
$(a_1 + 2d) + g_1 r^2 = 4$
$1 + 2d + r^2 = 4$
$2d + r^2 = 3$

Substituting $d = -r$ into the equation:
$-2r + r^2 = 3$
$r^2 - 2r - 3 = 0$
$(r - 3)(r + 1) = 0$

Since the G.P. is increasing and $g_1 = 1$, the common ratio $r$ must be greater than $1$. Thus, $r = 3$.

Then, $d = -3$.

We need to find $a_{10} + g_5$:
$a_{10} = a_1 + 9d = 1 + 9(-3) = -26$
$g_5 = g_1 r^4 = 1(3)^4 = 81$

$a_{10} + g_5 = -26 + 81 = 55$

Answer: $55$

38939.text: Using Bohr's model, calculate the ratio of the magnetic fields generated due to the motion of the electrons in the $2^{\text{nd}}$ and $4^{\text{th}}$ orbits of hydrogen atom _______.
38939.sol:
The magnetic field at the center of a circular orbit is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r}$.

The equivalent current due to the revolving electron is $I = \dfrac{e}{T} = \dfrac{ev}{2\pi r}$.

Substituting $I$ into the expression for $B$, we get $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 ev}{4\pi r^2}$.

According to Bohr's model for a hydrogen atom, the velocity of the electron in the $n^{\text{th}}$ orbit is $v \propto \dfrac{1}{n}$ and the radius of the orbit is $r \propto n^2$.

Therefore, the magnetic field $B$ depends on the principal quantum number $n$ as $B \propto \dfrac{1/n}{(n^2)^2} \Rightarrow B \propto \dfrac{1}{n^5}$.

The ratio of the magnetic fields in the $2^{\text{nd}}$ and $4^{\text{th}}$ orbits is $\dfrac{B_2}{B_4} = \left(\dfrac{n_4}{n_2}\right)^5 = \left(\dfrac{4}{2}\right)^5 = 2^5 = 32$.

Answer: $32$

39513.subject: Physics
39513.text: Refer to the figure given below, current between terminals $A$ and $B$ is _____ A.
39513.sol:
The given circuit consists of four parallel branches connected between the left and right common vertical wires.

Let's find the equivalent electromotive force (EMF) and resistance for each branch:
For the top three active branches, each contains three $5\text{ V}$ cells and three $3\ \Omega$ resistors in series.
Equivalent EMF of each active branch, $E = 5 + 5 + 5 = 15\text{ V}$.
Equivalent resistance of each active branch, $R = 3 + 3 + 3 = 9\ \Omega$.

Since these three identical active branches are connected in parallel, we can replace them with a single equivalent voltage source:
Equivalent EMF, $E_{eq} = 15\text{ V}$ (as they are identical and in parallel).
Equivalent internal resistance, $R_{eq} = \dfrac{9}{3} = 3\ \Omega$.

The fourth (bottom) branch is connected between terminals $A$ and $B$ and acts as the load for this equivalent source. It contains three $3\ \Omega$ resistors in series.
Resistance of the branch $AB$, $R_{AB} = 3 + 3 + 3 = 9\ \Omega$.

Now, the circuit is simplified to an equivalent source of $15\text{ V}$ with internal resistance $3\ \Omega$ connected across a load of $9\ \Omega$.
The current $I$ flowing between terminals $A$ and $B$ (through the bottom branch) is given by Ohm's law:
$I = \dfrac{E_{eq}}{R_{eq} + R_{AB}}$

$I = \dfrac{15}{3 + 9} = \dfrac{15}{12}\text{ A}$

$I = 1.25\text{ A}$

Answer: $1.25$

39518.subject: Physics
39518.text: A Wheatstone bridge is initially at room temperature and all arms of the bridge have same value of resistances $\left(R_{1}=R_{2}=R_{3}=R_{4}\right)$. When $R_{3}$ resistance is heated to some temperature, its resistance value has gone up by $10 \%$. The potential difference $\left(V_{a}-V_{b}\right)$ (after $R_{3}$ is heated) is $\_\_\_\_$ V.
39518.sol:
Initially, the Wheatstone bridge is balanced with $R_1 = R_2 = R_3 = R_4 = R$.
Since the bridge is balanced, the potential difference across the bridge is zero: $V_a - V_b = 0$ V.
When $R_3$ is heated and its resistance increases by 10%: $R_3' = 1.1R$
The voltage at node $a$ (between $R_1$ and $R_2$): $V_a = 40 \times \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} = 40 \times \frac{R}{R + R} = 40 \times \frac{1}{2} = 20$ V
The voltage at node $b$ (between $R_3'$ and $R_4$): $V_b = 40 \times \frac{R_4}{R_3' + R_4} = 40 \times \frac{R}{1.1R + R} = 40 \times \frac{1}{2.1} \approx 19.05$ V
Therefore: $V_a - V_b = 20 - 19.05 = 0.95$ V

42104.subject: Physics
42104.text: A wire of length $L$ and radius $r$ is clamped at one end. If its other end is pulled by a force $F$, its length increases by $l$. If the radius of the wire and the applied force both are reduced to half of their original values keeping original length constant, the increase in length will become:
42104.sol:
The formula to calculate the Young's modulus of the material of the wire, in the first case, can be written as

$Y = \dfrac{\dfrac{F}{\pi{r}^{2}}}{\dfrac{l}{L}} . . . \left(1\right)$

From equation (1), it follows that

$F = Y\pi{r}^{2} \times \dfrac{l}{L} . . . \left(2\right)$

For the second case, the Young's modulus is given by

$Y = \dfrac{\dfrac{F / 2}{\pi{r}^{2} / 4}}{\dfrac{l '}{L}} . . . \left(3\right)$

From equation (3), it follows that

$F = Y\dfrac{l '}{L} \times 2 \times \dfrac{\pi{r}^{2}}{4} . . . \left(4\right)$

From equations (2) and (4), it implies that

$Y\pi{r}^{2} \times \dfrac{l}{L} = Y\dfrac{l '}{L} \times 2 \times \dfrac{\pi{r}^{2}}{4} ⇒ l ' = 2l$

44441.text: An observer moves towards a stationary source of sound with a velocity one-fifth of the velocity of sound. The percentage change in the apparent frequency is
44441.sol:
By Doppler's effect
$\dfrac{{ν}^{'}}{ν} = \dfrac{c + {ν}_{0}}{c}$ (where $c$ is the velocity of sound)
$\dfrac{{ν}^{'}}{ν} = \dfrac{v + \left(v / 5\right)}{v} = \dfrac{6}{5}$
$∴$ Fractional increase$= \dfrac{{ν}^{'} - ν}{ν} = \left(\dfrac{{ν}^{'}}{ν} - 1\right) = \left(\dfrac{6}{5} - 1\right) = \dfrac{1}{5}$

$∴$ Percentage increase $= \dfrac{100}{5} = 20 %$

46290.subject: Physics
46290.text: A body at rest slides down a $30^{\circ}$ inclined plane. The time taken by it to slide down is twice the time it takes when it slides down the same distance in the absence of friction. The coefficient of friction between the body and the inclined plane is
46290.sol:
When a plane is inclined to the horizontal at an angle $\theta$, which is greater than the angle of repose, then the body placed on the inclined plane slides down with an acceleration a.

From figure,
$R=m g \cos \theta$.....(i)
Net force on the body down the inclined plane
$f=m g \sin \theta-F$....(ii)
i.e. $\quad f=m a=m g \sin \theta-\mu R \quad\left[\because \mu=\frac{F}{R}\right] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad m a & =m g \sin \theta-\mu m g \cos \theta \quad \text{ [from Eq. (i)] } \\ & =m g(\sin \theta-\mu \cos \theta) \\ \Rightarrow \quad a & =g(\sin \theta-\mu \cos \theta)\end{aligned}$
Time taken by the body to slide down the plane
$\begin{aligned} & t_1=\sqrt{\frac{2 s}{a}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 s}{(g \sin \theta-\mu g \cos \theta)}} \\ & t_2=\sqrt{\frac{2 s}{g \sin \theta}} \quad \text{ [in absence of friction] }\end{aligned} \because \quad t_1=2 t_2 \Rightarrow \quad t_1^2=4 t_2^2$
[given]
$\begin{aligned} & \left|\sqrt{\frac{2 s}{(g \sin \theta-\mu g \cos \theta)}}\right|^2=4 \times\left|\sqrt{\frac{2 s}{g \sin \theta}}\right|^2 \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{2 s}{g(\sin \theta-\mu \cos \theta)}=4 \times \frac{2 s}{g \sin \theta} \\ \Rightarrow & \quad \sin \theta=4 \sin \theta-4 \mu \cos \theta \\ \Rightarrow & \mu=\frac{3}{4} \tan \theta=\frac{3}{4} \tan 30^{\circ}=0.43\end{aligned}$

46647.text: The temperature of inversion of a thermocouple is $620^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and the neutral temperature is $300^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, what is the temperature of cold junction?
46647.sol:
The temperature of inversion is higher than the neutral temperature by the same amount as the neutral temperature is higher than the temperature of cold junction.
As per Key Idea
$t_n-t_0=t_i-t_n \Rightarrow t_0=2 t_n-t_i$
Given, $t_i=620^{\circ} \mathrm{C}, t_n=300^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$
Hence, $t_0=$ temperature of cold junction
$\begin{aligned} & =2 \times 300-620 \\ & =600-620=-20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\end{aligned}$
NOTE: Neutral temperature does not change for a metal whether the temperature of cold junction and inversion temperature change by any value.

Amnion is an extraembryonic membrane that surrounds embryo in reptiles, birds and mammals. It provides a kind of private aquarium to the embryo and protects it from mechanical shock and desiccation.
Chorion (serosa) is the outermost extra embryonic membrane in reptiles, birds and mammals. It surrounds the whole embryonic system of embryo.
Yolk sac contains yolk in reptiles and birds. In mammals, yolk sac is also known as umbilical vesicle. It is connected to enteron of embryo by a slender yolk stalk.

49692.text: If $\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}, \overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}$ and $\overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}}$ are unit vectors, such that $\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}+\overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}+\overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}}=\overrightarrow{\mathbf{0}}$, then $3 \overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}+2 \overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}}+\overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}$ is
49692.sol:
$\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}, \overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}, \overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}}$ are unit vectors, then $|\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}|=|\overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}|=|\overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}}|=1$
Given,

$\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}+\overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}+\overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}}&=0 \\
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}&=-(\overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}+\overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}})
\end{aligned}$ Squaring on both sides

$\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}^{2}}&=(\overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}+\overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}})^{2}\\
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}^{2}}&=\overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}^{2}}+\overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}^{2}}+2 \overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}}\\
|\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}|^{2}&=|\overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}|^{2}+|\overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}}|^{2}+2(\overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}}) \quad\left(\because \overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}^{2}}=|\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}|^{2}\right)
\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}&1=1+1+2(\overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}})\\
&\Rightarrow \overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}}=-1 / 2\\
&\text{ Similarly, } \overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}=\overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}=-1 / 2\\
&\text{ Hence, }3 \overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}+2 \overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}}+\overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}\\
&=3(-1 / 2)+2(-1 / 2)+(-1 / 2)\\
&=(3+2+1)(-1 / 2)\\
&=6(-1 / 2)=-3
\end{aligned}
$

options: A observes both electric and magnetic fields

50100.sol:
For observer A sitting in the train, the point charge is at rest. A stationary charge produces only an electric field. Thus, A observes only an electric field.

For observer B standing on the ground, the point charge is moving with the velocity of the train. A moving charge produces both an electric field and a magnetic field. Thus, B observes both electric and magnetic fields.

Answer: B observes both electric and magnetic fields

50752.text:
A carnot engine takes \( 300 \) calories of heat from a source at \( 500 $\mathrm{ K}$\) and rejects \( 150 \) calories of
heat to the sink. The temperature of the sink is
50752.sol:
Given, heat taken from source, $Q_{1}=300$ calories; temperature of source $T_{1}=500 \mathrm{ K} ;$ heat rejected to the
sink, $Q_{2}=150$ calories.
Temperature of sink, $T_{2}=?$
Now, efficiency, $\eta=\frac{Q_{1}-Q_{2}}{Q}$
Also, efficiency, $\eta=\frac{T_{1}-T_{2}}{T_{1}}$
Therefore, $\frac{Q_{1}-Q_{2}}{Q_{1}}=\frac{T_{1}-T_{2}}{T_{1}}\Rightarrow \frac{300-150}{300}=\frac{500-T_{2}}{500}\Rightarrow \frac{150}{300}=1-\frac{T_{2}}{500}\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2}=1-\frac{T_{2}}{500}\Rightarrow \frac{T_{2}}{500}=1-\frac{1}{2}\Rightarrow T_{2}=500 \times \frac{1}{2}=250 \mathrm{ K}$
Thus, temperature of sink $=250 \mathrm{ K}$

55454.subject: Chemistry
55454.text: Which one of the following is a globular protein?
55454.sol:
Proteins are classified into fibrous and globular proteins based on their molecular shape.

Fibrous proteins have a fiber-like structure formed by parallel polypeptide chains held together by hydrogen and disulfide bonds. Examples include keratin (found in hair, wool, silk) and myosin (found in muscles).

Globular proteins have a spherical shape formed when the chains of polypeptides coil around. Examples include insulin and albumins.

Thus, insulin is a globular protein.

Answer: Insulin

56021.text: What is numerical value of rate constant of a first order reaction that is $20 \%$ completed in 10 minute ?
56021.sol:
The integrated rate law for a first-order reaction is $k = \frac{2.303}{t} \log \left(\frac{[A]_0}{[A]_t}\right).

Since the reaction is 20% complete after 10 minutes, $[A]_t = 0.8[A]_0$. Choosing $[A]_0 = 100$ and $[A]_t = 80$ gives \frac{[A]_0}{[A]_t} =1.25$.

$k = \frac{2.303}{10} \log(1.25) $\approx$0.2303 \times0.0969 $\approx$0.02231 \text{ min}^{-1}$

This matches option A.

Which from following is a currect representation of reaction rate for reaction stated below?
$\mathrm{N}_{2(\mathrm{ g})}+3 \mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{ g})} \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NH}_{3(\mathrm{ g})}$
56058.sol:
The rate of reaction for a general equation $\mathrm{aA} + \mathrm{bB} \rightarrow \mathrm{cC} + \mathrm{dD}$ is defined as

$\text{Rate} = -\frac{1}{\mathrm{a}}\frac{\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{A}]}{\mathrm{dt}} = -\frac{1}{\mathrm{b}}\frac{\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{B}]}{\mathrm{dt}} = +\frac{1}{\mathrm{c}}\frac{\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{C}]}{\mathrm{dt}} = +\frac{1}{\mathrm{d}}\frac{\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{D}]}{\mathrm{dt}}$

For $\mathrm{N}_{2(\mathrm{g})} + 3\mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{g})} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH}_{3(\mathrm{g})}$, the stoichiometric coefficients are 1, 3, and 2 respectively, giving

$\text{Rate} = -\frac{\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{N}_2]}{\mathrm{dt}} = -\frac{1}{3}\frac{\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{H}_2]}{\mathrm{dt}} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{NH}_3]}{\mathrm{dt}}$

Comparing with the options, only

C) $-\frac{\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{N}_2]}{\mathrm{dt}} = -\frac{1}{3}\frac{\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{H}_2]}{\mathrm{dt}} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{NH}_3]}{\mathrm{dt}}$

matches the derived expression.

The correct answer is $\boxed{\text{C}}$.

57615.subject: Chemistry
57615.text: Which among the following is vinylic halide?
57615.sol:
Definition of Vinylic Halide: An organic compound where a halogen atom (X$) is bonded directly to an sp^2$ hybridized carbon that is part of a carbon–carbon double bond (C=C$).

A) Haloalkane: The halogen is bonded to an sp^3$ hybridized carbon, as in chloroethane (CH_3CH_2Cl$), which does not satisfy the definition.

B) Haloalkene: Includes structures where the halogen is attached to a carbon in an alkene. Vinylic halides (e.g., chloroethene, $CH_2=CH-Cl$) are a subset, with the halogen on an sp^2$ carbon of the double bond.

C) Haloalkyne: The halogen is bonded to an sp hybridized carbon in a triple bond, such as chloroethyne (CH\equiv C-Cl$), not meeting the criteria.

D) Haloarene: The halogen is on an sp^2$ carbon in an aromatic ring (e.g., chlorobenzene, $C_6H_5Cl$), but “vinylic” specifically denotes non-aromatic alkenes.

Thus, vinylic halides are a type of haloalkene, making B the correct classification.

Final answer: $\boxed{B}$

59172.subject: Chemistry
59172.text:
Calculate the percent dissociation of 0.02 m solution if its freezing point
depression is 0.046 K
$\left[\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{f}}\right.$ for water $\left.=1.86 \mathrm{~K} \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} ; \mathrm{n}=2\right]$
59172.sol:
The percent dissociation is determined using freezing point depression data. The van't Hoff factor $i$ is calculated as $i = \frac{\Delta T_f}{K_f \cdot m} = \frac{0.046}{1.86 \cdot 0.02} \approx 1.23656$.

For a substance dissociating into two ions, $i = 1 + (2 - 1)\alpha$. Substituting gives $1.23656 = 1 + \alpha$, so $\alpha \approx 0.23656$.

The percent dissociation is therefore $0.23656 \times 100\% \approx 23.656\%$, which rounds to $23.7\%$. The closest option is $\boxed{\text{B}}$.

59542.text: A gas at $10\,^{}^{\circ}\text{C}$ occupies a volume of 283 mL. if it is heated to $20\,^{}^{\circ}\text{C}$ keeping the pressure constant. What is the new volume of gas ?
59542.sol:
According to Charles's Law, at constant pressure, $\dfrac{V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{V_2}{T_2}$

Given:
$V_1 = 283 \text{ mL}$
$T_1 = 10\,^{}^{\circ}\text{C} = 10 + 273 = 283 \text{ K}$
$T_2 = 20\,^{}^{\circ}\text{C} = 20 + 273 = 293 \text{ K}$

Substituting the values:
$\dfrac{283}{283} = \dfrac{V_2}{293}$

$V_2 = 293 \text{ mL}$

Answer: $293 \text{ mL}$

59897.text: The enthalpy of combustion of cyclohexane, cyclohexene and $\text{H}_2$ are respectively $-3920, -3800$ and $-241$ KJ mol^{-1}$. The enthalpy of hydrogenation of cyclohexene is$
59897.sol:
The hydrogenation reaction of cyclohexene is given by:

$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10} + \text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}$

The enthalpy of hydrogenation can be calculated using the enthalpies of combustion of the reactants and products:

$\Delta H = \sum \Delta H_c(\text{reactants}) - \sum \Delta H_c(\text{products})$

$\Delta H = [\Delta H_c(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}) + \Delta H_c(\text{H}_2)] - \Delta H_c(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12})$

60402.text: If slope of a tangent to the curve $x y+a x+b y=0$ at the point $(1,1)$ on it is 2 , then $a-b$ is
60402.sol:
Given curve is
$\begin{aligned}
& x y+\mathrm{a} x+\mathrm{b} y=0 \\
\therefore \quad & \text{ Slope }=2=\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{ d} x} \\
\therefore \quad & x y+\mathrm{a} x+\mathrm{b} y=0
\end{aligned}$
Differentiating w.r.t. $x$, we get
$\begin{aligned}
& x \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{ d} x}+y+\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b} \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{ d} x}=0 \\
& \therefore \quad(x+\mathrm{b}) \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{ d} x}=-(y+\mathrm{a}) \\
& \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{ d} x}=\frac{-(y+\mathrm{a})}{x+\mathrm{b}} \\
& \therefore \quad\left(\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{ d} x}\right)_{(1,1)}=2 \\
& \therefore \quad 2=\frac{-(1+\mathrm{a})}{1+\mathrm{b}} \\
& \therefore \quad \mathrm{a}+2 \mathrm{ b}=-3 ... (i)
\end{aligned}$
Since $(1,1)$ lies on $x y+a x+b y=0$, we get $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}=-1$ ... (ii)
Solving (i), (ii), we get
$\begin{aligned}
& a=1, b=-2 \\
\therefore \quad & a-b=1-(-2)=3
\end{aligned}$

options: $\left(\dfrac{x + \log x}{x}\right)^2 + c$, where c is the constant of integration

62177.sol:
Let $I = \displaystyle\int \dfrac{(x + 1)(x + \log x)^2}{x} \, dx$

$I = \displaystyle\int \left( 1 + \dfrac{1}{x} \right) (x + \log x)^2 \, dx$

Substituting $x + \log x = t$

Differentiating with respect to $x$,

$\left( 1 + \dfrac{1}{x} \right) dx = dt$

Substituting $t and dt$ into the integral,

$I = \displaystyle\int t^2 \, dt$

$I = \dfrac{t^3}{3} + c$

Substituting back $t = x + \log x$,

$I = \dfrac{(x + \log x)^3}{3} + c$

Answer: $\dfrac{(x + \log x)^3}{3} + c$, where c is the constant of integration

The following is the probability distribution of X
X 0 1 2 3
$P(X=x)$ $\frac{1+p}{5}$ $\frac{2-2 p}{5}$ $\frac{2-p}{5}$ $\frac{2 p}{5}$

The probability distribution remains valid when all probabilities are non-negative. This requires $P(X=0) = \frac{1+p}{5} \geq 0$ implying $p \geq -1$, $P(X=1) = \frac{2-2p}{5} \geq 0$ implying $p \leq 1$, $P(X=2) = \frac{2-p}{5} \geq 0$ implying $p \leq 2$, and $P(X=3) = \frac{2p}{5} \geq 0$ implying $p \geq 0$.

Combining these inequalities yields the valid range $0 \leq p \leq 1$.

The minimum value of $p$ is therefore $0$. Substituting $p = 0$ gives the distribution:
$P(X=0) = \frac{1}{5}$, $P(X=1) = \frac{2}{5}$, $P(X=2) = \frac{2}{5}$, $P(X=3) = 0$.

The expected value is calculated as:
$E(X) = 0 \cdot \frac{1}{5} + 1 \cdot \frac{2}{5} + 2 \cdot \frac{2}{5} + 3 \cdot 0 = \frac{2}{5} + \frac{4}{5} = \frac{6}{5}$.

Multiplying by 5 gives $5E(X) = 5 \cdot \frac{6}{5} = 6$.

64944.subject: Mathematics
64944.text: If $\cos(\theta-\alpha)=a$ and $\sin(\theta-\beta)=b$, then the value of $\cos^2(\alpha-\beta)+2ab\sin(\alpha-\beta)+\cos^2(\theta-\alpha)$ is...
64944.sol:
Let $x = \theta - \alpha$ and $y = \theta - \beta$.

Given $\cos x = a$ and $\sin y = b$.

We can write $\alpha - \beta = (\theta - \beta) - (\theta - \alpha) = y - x$.

Using the trigonometric expansion formulas:

$\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos(y - x) = \cos y \cos x + \sin y \sin x = a \cos y + b \sin x$

$\sin(\alpha - \beta) = \sin(y - x) = \sin y \cos x - \cos y \sin x = ab - \cos y \sin x$

Substituting these into the given expression $\cos^2(\alpha-\beta)+2ab\sin(\alpha-\beta)+\cos^2(\theta-\alpha)$:

$(a \cos y + b \sin x)^2 + 2ab(ab - \cos y \sin x) + a^2$

Expanding the terms, we get:

$a^2 \cos^2 y + b^2 \sin^2 x + 2ab \cos y \sin x + 2a^2b^2 - 2ab \cos y \sin x + a^2$

Canceling $2ab \cos y \sin x$ and expressing $\cos^2 y$ and $\sin^2 x$ in terms of $a$ and $b$:

$a^2(1 - \sin^2 y) + b^2(1 - \cos^2 x) + 2a^2b^2 + a^2$

Since $\sin y = b$ and $\cos x = a$, this becomes:

$a^2(1 - b^2) + b^2(1 - a^2) + 2a^2b^2 + a^2$

$a^2 - a^2b^2 + b^2 - a^2b^2 + 2a^2b^2 + a^2$

Simplifying the expression, the terms with $a^2b^2$ cancel out:

$a^2 + b^2 + a^2 = 2a^2 + b^2$

Answer: $2a^2 + b^2$

66350.text: If the length of the potentiometer wire is increased by keeping constant potential difference across the wire, then
options: the null point is obtained at shorter distance.
the null point is obtained at larger distance.
there is no change in the null point.
66350.sol:
The potential gradient $k$ represents the potential drop per unit length and is defined by $k = V / L$ where $V$ is the potential difference across the potentiometer wire and $L$ is the total wire length.

Since $V$ remains constant while $L$ increases, the potential gradient $k$ must decrease, making option B incorrect.

For an unknown electromotive force $E$ balanced by the potentiometer, the null point occurs at length $l$ satisfying $E = k \cdot l$. Substituting the expression for $k$ yields $E = (V / L) \cdot l$, which rearranges to $l = E \cdot (L / V)$.

With both $E$ and $V$ constant, increasing $L$ causes $l$ to increase proportionally. The null point therefore occurs at a larger distance.

Final answer: $\boxed{C}$

68046.subject: Physics
68046.text: The formula for the physical quantity is $\mathrm{P}=\frac{\mathrm{x}^3 \mathrm{y}}{\mathrm{z}^2}$ and the percentage error in the determination of physical quantities $x, y, z$ are $0.6 \%, 3 \%$ and $1.3 \%$ respectively. The percentage error in the measurement of $P$ is
68046.sol:
The physical quantity is given as $P = \frac{x^3 y}{z^2}$ or equivalently $P = x^3 y^1 z^{-2}$.

For quantities involving products and powers, the maximum percentage error is given by:

$\left|3\frac{\Delta x}{x} + 1\frac{\Delta y}{y} + 2\frac{\Delta z}{z}\right| \times 100\%$

with the measured percentage errors $\frac{\Delta x}{x} \times 100\% = 0.6\%$, $\frac{\Delta y}{y} \times 100\% = 3\%$, and $\frac{\Delta z}{z} \times 100\% = 1.3\%$.

Substituting these values:

$\frac{\Delta P}{P} \times 100\% = 3(0.6\%) + 1(3\%) + 2(1.3\%)$

$= 1.8\% + 3\% + 2.6\% = 7.4\%$

The percentage error in $P$ is $7.4\%$, corresponding to option D.

68512.subject: Physics
68512.text: Two girls are standing at the ends 'A' and 'B' of a ground where $A B=b$. The girl at ' $B$ ' starts running in a direction perpendicular to ' AB ' with velocity ' $\mathrm{V}_1$ '. The girl at 'A' starts running simultaneously with velocity ' $\mathrm{V}_2$ ' and in shortest distance meets the other girl in time ' t '. The value of ' $t$ ' is
68512.sol:
Establish a coordinate system where girl A starts at $(0,0)$ and girl B at $(b,0)$. Girl B runs perpendicular to AB with velocity $V_1$, placing her position at time $t$ at $(b, V_1 t)$.

Girl A runs directly toward this meeting point with velocity $V_2$. The distance traveled by A is the straight-line distance between initial positions, given by the Pythagorean theorem:

$(V_2 t)^2 = b^2 + (V_1 t)^2$

Solving for $t$:

$V_2^2 t^2 - V_1^2 t^2 = b^2$
$t^2 (V_2^2 - V_1^2) = b^2$
$t = \frac{b}{\sqrt{V_2^2 - V_1^2}}$

This solution requires $V_2 > V_1$ for real $t$. The expression matches option D.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{D}}$

When an exotic species is introduced accidentally or intentionally into a new geographical area, it often becomes invasive and starts spreading rapidly.

71101.subject: Biology
71101.text: Which of the following epochs marks the major radiation of modern birds?
71101.sol:
The question asks for the epoch that marks the major radiation of modern birds.

The extinction of non-avian dinosaurs at the end of the Cretaceous period (Mesozoic era) left many ecological niches vacant. In the subsequent Cenozoic era, modern birds (Neornithes) underwent a rapid and massive evolutionary radiation to fill these niches.

The Palaeocene epoch (the first epoch of the Cenozoic era) is widely recognized in evolutionary biology and paleontology as the time when the major adaptive radiation of modern birds occurred, leading to the establishment of most of the major lineages of birds we see today.

Answer: Palaeocene

71777.text: Find the molar conductivity of $0.001$M $\text{AgNO}_3$ solution if the conductivity of it is $1.2 \times 10^{-4}\Omega^{-1}$ cm^{-1}$.$

Concentration, $M = 0.001 \text{ M}$

72274.subject: Physics
72274.text: Magnetic susceptibility (\chi$) is related to magnetic relative permeability (\mu_r$) by the relation
72274.sol:
The magnetic permeability of a material is given by $\mu = \mu_0 (1 + \chi)$, where $\chi$ is the magnetic susceptibility.

The relative magnetic permeability is defined as $\mu_r = \dfrac{\mu}{\mu_0}$.

Substituting this into the first equation gives $\mu_r = 1 + \chi$.

Rearranging the terms, we get $\chi = \mu_r - 1$.

Answer: $\chi = \mu_r - 1$

76424.text:
Consider the following for the two (02) items that follow:
The slope of the tangent to the curve $y = f(x)$ at $(x, f(x))$ is 4 for every real number $x$ and the curve passes through the origin.

What is the area bounded by the curve, the $x$-axis and the line $x = 4$?
76424.sol:
Given $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 4$

Integrating both sides, $y = 4x + C$

Since the curve passes through the origin $(0,0)$, we have $0 = 4(0) + C \Rightarrow C = 0$

The equation of the curve is $y = 4x$

The area bounded by the curve, the $x$-axis and the line $x = 4$ is given by $\int_{0}^{4} y \, dx$

Area $= \int_{0}^{4} 4x \, dx = \left[ 2x^2 \right]_{0}^{4} = 2(16) - 0 = 32$ square units.

Answer: $32$ square units

76648.text: If $z \neq 0$ is a complex number, then what is $\text{amp}(z) + \text{amp}(\bar{z})$ equal to?
76648.sol:
Let $z = r(\cos \theta + i\sin \theta)$ where $r > 0$ and $\theta = \text{amp}(z)$.

The conjugate of $z$ is given by $\bar{z} = r(\cos \theta - i\sin \theta)$.

This can be rewritten as $\bar{z} = r(\cos(-\theta) + i\sin(-\theta))$.

Thus, the amplitude of $\bar{z}$ is $\text{amp}(\bar{z}) = -\theta$.

Therefore, $\text{amp}(z) + \text{amp}(\bar{z}) = \theta + (-\theta) = 0$.

Answer: $0$

80533.subject: Botany
80533.text: Even in absence of pollinating agents seed-setting is assured in
80533.sol: Commellina benghalensis or kankauoa bears aerial, chasmogamous (stigma and anthers exposed to pollinating agents), insect pollinated flowers and underground cleistogamous flowers. Cleistogamous flowers are bisexual flowers which never open, i.e., always remain closed. In such flowers the anthers and stigma lie very close to each other. When anthers dehisce in the flower buds, pollen grains come in contact with the stigma of the same flower, i.e., autogamy occurs. So, these flowers produce assured seed set, even in the absence of pollinators.

80784.subject: Chemistry
80784.text: Alpha-helix is found in which level of protein structure ?
80784.sol:
The primary structure of a protein refers to the linear sequence of amino acids.

The secondary structure refers to the local folded structures that form within a polypeptide due to interactions between atoms of the backbone. The most common types of secondary structures are the $\alpha$-helix and the $\beta$-pleated sheet.

The tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional structure of a polypeptide.

The quaternary structure is the arrangement of multiple folded protein or coiling protein molecules in a multi-subunit complex.

Therefore, the $\alpha$-helix is found in the secondary structure of proteins.

Answer: Secondary structure

81793.text:
What fraction of $\mathrm{Fe}$ exists as $\mathrm{Fe}$ (III) in $\mathrm{Fe}_{0.96} \mathrm{O}$ ?
(Consider $\mathrm{Fe}_{0.96}$ to be made up of $\mathrm{Fe}$ (II) and $\mathrm{Fe}$ (III) only)
81793.sol:
Let's assume $\mathrm{Fe}$ in $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}=\mathrm{x}$
Let's assume $\mathrm{Fe}$ in $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}(0.96-x)$
Using the charge conservation formula for
$\mathrm{Fe}_{0.96} \mathrm{O}_{1.00}$
We get: $(x)(+2)+(0.96-x)(+3)-2=0 \begin{aligned}
& =2 x+2.88-3 x-2=0 \\
& x=0.88
\end{aligned}$
So, number of ions of $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}=0.96-x=0.96-0.88=0.08 \text{Fraction of } \mathrm{Fe}^{3+} \text{ ion } =\frac{0.08}{0.96} =\frac{1}{12}$

84613.text: Given below are two statements regarding oogenesis. Statement I : The primary follicles get surrounded by more layers of granulosa cells, a theca and shows fluid filled cavity antrum. Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is true

Option (4) is the answer because, each primary follicle gets surrounded by more layers of granulosa cells and a new theca and are called secondary follicles. The Graafian follicle now ruptures to release the secondary oocyte (ovum) from the ovary by the process called ovulation.
So, the statement I is incorrect but statement II is correct.

92649.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
92649.text: Two identical spheres, each of mass $m$ are suspended by vertical strings such& that they are in contact with& their centres at the same level. A third identical& sphere strikes the other two spheres& simultaneously with a velocity $u$& such that& the centres of the spheres at the instant of impact form an equilateral triangle in a vertical plane. If the collision is perfectly elastic, then the combined impulse due to the strings is
92649.sol:
Let us assume that after the collision, the velocity of the incoming ball changes from& $u$~to& $u^{'}$~and the other two balls move in the opposite directions with the same speed& $v$, then

$- 2\left(N ∆ t\right)cos30 ° = mu^{'} - mu$

$⇒ - \left(N ∆ t\right)\sqrt{3} = mu^{'} - mu$

For the ball attached to the string,

$\left(N ∆ t\right)sin30 ° = mv$

$⇒ N ∆ t = 2mv$

Eliminating~$N ∆ t$, we obtain

$- 2\sqrt{3}mv = mu^{'} - mu$

Using the coefficient of restitution equation we get

$1 = \dfrac{vcos60 ° - u^{'}cos30 °}{ucos30 °}$

$⇒ \sqrt{3}u = v - \sqrt{3}u^{'}$

$⇒ 2\sqrt{3}v = 6u + 6u^{'}$

$6u + 6u^{'} = u - u^{'}$

$⇒ u^{'} = - \dfrac{5}{7}u$

The total impulse of tension is

$- 2T ∆ t = mu^{'} - mu$

$2T ∆ t = m\dfrac{5u}{7} + mu = \dfrac{12}{7}mu$

for second case image distance should be same

$\dfrac{1}{\text{v}} + \dfrac{1}{5 0} = \dfrac{1}{{f ⁡}_{2}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{2 5} - \dfrac{1}{5 0} = \dfrac{1}{{f ⁡}_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{{f ⁡}_{2}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{1 {cm}^{- 1}}{5 0} = \dfrac{1}{{f ⁡}_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{{f ⁡}_{2}} = {\text{P}}_{1} - {\text{P}}_{2} = 2 \text{D}$

Let power of his eye lens in two cases are (Pe)1, (Pe)2 respectively

${\text{P}}_{1} = \left(\text{2.5} + {\left({\text{P}}_{\text{e}}\right)}_{1}\right)$

${\text{P}}_{2} = \left(\text{2.5} + {\left({\text{P}}_{\text{e}}\right)}_{2}\right)$

$⇒ {\text{P}}_{1} - {\text{P}}_{2} = {\left({\text{P}}_{\text{e}}\right)}_{1} - {\left({\text{P}}_{\text{e}}\right)}_{2}$

= 2 D

So loss in power is 2 D so he should use additional power of 2 D i.e. 4.5 D

93236.text: There is a crater of depth $\dfrac{R}{100}$ on the surface of the moon, where $R$ is the radius of the moon. A ball is projected vertically upwards from the crater with a velocity which is equal to the escape velocity from the surface of the moon. If the maximum height attained by the particle is close to $nR$, where $n$ is an integer, then find the value of $n$?
93236.sol:
Speed of particle at $A$,

${v}_{A} = v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$

At point $B, {v}_{B} = 0$

By conservation of energy,

decrease in $KE =$ increase in GPE

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{2}{Mv}_{Λ}^{2} = {U}_{B} - {U}_{A}$

$∴ \dfrac{1}{2}M \cdot \left(\dfrac{2GM}{R}\right) = M\left({V}_{B} - {V}_{A}\right)$

$∴ \dfrac{GM}{R} = - \dfrac{GM}{R + h} - \left[\dfrac{- GM}{2R}\left[3 - \dfrac{\left{\left(R - \dfrac{R}{100}\right)}^{2}\right]}{{R}^{2}}\right]\right)

$∴ \dfrac{1}{R} = - \dfrac{1}{R + h} + \dfrac{3}{2R} - \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right){\left(\dfrac{99}{100}\right)}^{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{R}$

$∴ \dfrac{1}{R} = - \dfrac{1}{R + h} + \dfrac{3}{2R} - \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\left(\dfrac{0 . 98}{R}\right)$$∴ \dfrac{1}{R + h} = \dfrac{1}{2R} [ 1 - 0 . 98 ]$

$∴ 2R = 0 . 02 ( R + h )$

$∴ h = \dfrac{1 . 98}{0 . 02}$

$∴ h = 99R$

94677.text: One mole of a monoatomic ideal gas undergoes the process $A ⟶ B$, as in the given $P - V$ diagram. The specific heat for this process is
94677.sol:
$\DeltaQ = \DeltaU + W$ (From ${1}^{st}$ law)

Here, $\DeltaU = n{C}_{V}\DeltaT$

Temperature at $A$,

${T}_{A} = \dfrac{2{P}_{0}{V}_{0}}{R}$

At $B$, ${T}_{B} = \dfrac{16{P}_{0}{V}_{0}}{R}$

So, $\DeltaU = \dfrac{3}{2}R\left[\dfrac{14{P}_{0}{V}_{0}}{R}\right] = 21{P}_{0}{V}_{0}$

$W = \left(2{P}_{0}\right)\left(3{V}_{0}\right) + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(3{V}_{0}\right)\left(2{P}_{0}\right)$   [Area under $P - V$ diagram]

$= 9{P}_{0}{V}_{0}$

So, $\DeltaQ = 21{P}_{0}{V}_{0} + 9{P}_{0}{V}_{0}$

$= 30{P}_{0}{V}_{0}$

$\DeltaQ = nC\DeltaT$

$C = \dfrac{\DeltaQ}{n\DeltaT} = \dfrac{30{P}_{0}{V}_{0}}{\dfrac{14{P}_{0}{V}_{0}}{R}} = \dfrac{15}{7}R$

97851.subject: Botany
97851.text:
Read the following statements and select the correct option.

a. To facilitate more sound and scientific placement of various taxa, taxonomists have also developed subcategories.
b. Only a few protozoans are heterotrophs and live as predators or parasites.
97851.sol:
Taxonomists have developed subcategories to make the taxonomic position of species more precise and specific categories are added to this list. They are called intermediate categories, e.g., subkingdom, superphylum or superdivision, subdivision, superclass, subclass, superorder, suborder, and superfamily subfamily, tribe, subspecies, variety etc.

All protozoans are compulsorily heterotrophic. They derive nutrients from other organisms, by completely ingesting the left out organic remains or waste-products. The protozoans perform phagocytosis and engulf their organic particles by forming pseudopodia or directly taking food through a specialized mouth called cytostome. Protozoans are basically free-living and often found in fresh, brackish, or saltwater. Parasitic and symbiotic protozoans are also present and they live within other organisms.

102027.subject: Physics
102027.text:
List I describes thermodynamic processes in four different systems. List II gives the magnitudes (either exactly or as a close approximation) of possible changes in the internal energy of the system due to the process.

  List-I   List-II
(I) ${10}^{- 3}kg$ of water $100 ° C$ is converted to steam at the same temperature, at a pressure of ${10}^{5}Pa$. The volume of the system changes from ${10}^{- 6}{m}^{3}$ to ${10}^{- 3}{m}^{3}$ in the process. Latent heat of water $= 2250kJ{kg}^{- 1}$ (P) $2kJ$
(II) $0 . 2$ moles of a rigid diatomic ideal gas with volume $V$ at temperature $500K$ undergoes an isobaric expansion to volume $3V$. Assume $8 . 0J{mol}^{– 1}{K}^{– 1}$ (Q) $7kJ$
(III) One mole of a monoatomic ideal gas is compressed adiabatically from volume $V = \dfrac{1}{3}{m}^{3}$ and pressure $2kPa$ to volume $\dfrac{V}{8}$. (R) $4kJ$
(IV) Three moles of a diatomic ideal gas whose molecules can vibrate, is given $9kJ$ of heat and undergoes isobaric expansion. (S) $5kJ$
    (T) $3kJ$

Which one of the following options is correct?
options: $I \to T, II \to R, III \to S, IV \to Q$
$I \to S, II \to P, III \to T, IV \to P$
$I \to P, II \to R, III \to T, IV \to Q$
$I \to Q, II \to R, III \to S, IV \to T$
102027.sol:
(I)

According to the first law of thermodynamics,

$∆ Q = ∆ U + W ⇒ ∆ U = ∆ Q - W$

$⇒ U = ML - P\DeltaV$

$= {10}^{- 3} \times 2250 - {10}^{2}kP \times \left({10}^{- 3} - {10}^{- 6}\right){m}^{3}$

$= 2 . 25kJ - 0 . 1kJ$

$= 2 . 15kJ$

Therefore, I-P

(II)

For isobaric process,

$\dfrac{{V}_{1}}{{V}_{2}} = \dfrac{{T}_{1}}{{T}_{2}} ⇒ {T}_{2} = 3 \times 500 = 1500K$

Now the change in the internal energy will be,

$∆ U = n{C}_{V} ∆ T = 0 . 2 \times \dfrac{5}{2} \times 8 \times 1000 = 4kJ$

Therefore, II-R

(III) 

For adiabatic expansion of monoatomic gas $\left(\gamma = \dfrac{5}{3}\right)$

${P}_{1}{V}_{1}^{\gamma} = {P}_{2}{V}_{2}^{\gamma} ⇒ \left(2kPa\right) \times {V}_{0}^{\dfrac{5}{3}} = {P}_{2} \times \left(\dfrac{{V}_{0}}{8}\right)\dfrac{5}{3}$

$⇒ {P}_{2} = 64kPa$

Now the change in the internal energy will be,

$\DeltaU = n{C}_{v}\DeltaT$

$= \dfrac{3nR\DeltaT}{2} = \dfrac{3}{2}\left({P}_{2}{V}_{2} - {P}_{1}{V}_{1}\right) = \dfrac{3}{2} \times \left(64 \times \dfrac{1}{3 \times 8} - 2 \times \dfrac{1}{3}\right)$

$= \dfrac{3}{2} \times \left(\dfrac{8}{3} - \dfrac{2}{3}\right) = 3kJ$

Therefore, III-T

(IV)

For diatomic gas whose molecules vibrate,

${C}_{V} = \dfrac{6}{2}R$ and ${C}_{P} = \dfrac{8}{2}R$

$⇒ \DeltaU = n{C}_{V}\DeltaT = 3nR\DeltaT$

$\DeltaQ = n{C}_{p}\DeltaT = 4nR\DeltaT$

$\dfrac{\DeltaU}{\DeltaQ} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

$\DeltaU = \dfrac{3}{4} \times 9 = 6 . 75 ≃ 7kJ$

Therefore, IV-Q

102069.subject: Physics
102069.text: An ideal gas is compressed from an initial volume $V_{0}$ to a final volume $\dfrac{V_{0}}{2}$ starting from the same initial state $(P_{0}, V_{0})$. The compression is carried out along two different paths, represented by curves A and B on a P-V diagram. If curve A lies above curve B (i.e., curve A ends at a higher pressure than curve B), which of the following correctly identifies the two processes?
options: Curve A is adiabatic and curve B is isothermal
Curve A is isothermal and curve B is adiabatic
Both curves represent isothermal processes at different temperatures
Both curves represent adiabatic processes for different gases
102069.sol:
The slope of a P-V curve is given by $\dfrac{dP}{dV}$.

For an isothermal process, the slope is $-\dfrac{P}{V}$.

For an adiabatic process, the slope is $-\gamma\dfrac{P}{V}$.

Since $\gamma > 1$, the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isothermal curve.

During compression, the volume decreases. Starting from the same initial state, the steeper adiabatic curve will rise more rapidly than the isothermal curve. Therefore, the adiabatic curve will lie above the isothermal curve on the P-V diagram, reaching a higher final pressure.

Since curve A ends at a higher pressure than curve B, curve A represents the adiabatic process and curve B represents the isothermal process.

Answer: Curve A is adiabatic and curve B is isothermal

103322.subject: Physics
103322.text: A uniform resistance wire AB of resistance $R_0$ is connected across an ideal DC voltage source of $V_0$. A resistor of unknown resistance $R$ is connected between end A and the midpoint C of the wire. If the measured potential difference across the resistor $R$ is $\dfrac{V_0}{4}$, what is the value of $R$ in terms of $R_0$?
103322.sol:
The wire AB is divided into two equal halves, AC and CB, each having a resistance of $\dfrac{R_0}{2}$.

The resistor $R$ is in parallel with the segment AC. The equivalent resistance of this parallel combination is:
$R_{AC} = \dfrac{R \times \dfrac{R_0}{2}}{R + \dfrac{R_0}{2}} = \dfrac{R R_0}{2R + R_0}$

The total resistance of the circuit is the sum of $R_{AC}$ and the resistance of segment CB:
$R_{eq} = R_{AC} + R_{CB} = \dfrac{R R_0}{2R + R_0} + \dfrac{R_0}{2} = \dfrac{4R R_0 + R_0^2}{2(2R + R_0)}$

The potential difference across the parallel combination (and thus across $R$) is given by the voltage divider rule:
$V_{AC} = V_0 \times \dfrac{R_{AC}}{R_{eq}} = V_0 \times \dfrac{\dfrac{R R_0}{2R + R_0}}{\dfrac{4R R_0 + R_0^2}{2(2R + R_0)}} = V_0 \left( \dfrac{2R}{4R + R_0} \right)$

We are given that $V_{AC} = \dfrac{V_0}{4}$. Equating the two expressions:
$\dfrac{V_0}{4} = V_0 \left( \dfrac{2R}{4R + R_0} \right)$
$\dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{2R}{4R + R_0}$
$4R + R_0 = 8R$
$4R = R_0 \Rightarrow R = \dfrac{R_0}{4}$

Answer: $\dfrac{R_0}{4}$

104798.subject: Physics
104798.text:
The graph which depicts the results of Rutherford gold foil experiment with $\alpha$ -particles is:
$\theta:$ Scattering angle
$Y:$ Number of scattered $\alpha$ -particles detected
(Plots are schematic and not to scale)
104798.sol:
Rutherford carried out an experiment in which he bombarded a thin sheet of gold foil with $\alpha$-particles and then analysed the trajectory of these particles after they collided with the gold foil.

For a detector at a specific angle with respect to the incident beam, the number of particles per unit area striking the detector is given by the Rutherford formula,

$Y\left(\theta\right) = \dfrac{{N}_{i}nL{Z}^{2}{k}^{2}{e}^{4}}{4{r}^{2}{\left(KE\right)}^{2}\sin^{4}\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right)}$

Here, ${N}_{i} =$ Number of incident alpha particles,

$n =$ Atoms per unit volume in target,

$L =$ Thickness of target,

$Z =$ Atomic number of target,

$e =$ Electron charge,

$k =$ Coulomb's constant,

$r =$ Distance between target and detector,

$KE =$ Kinetic energy of alpha particles,

$\theta =$ Scattering angle.

Therefore, $Y ∝ \dfrac{1}{\sin^{4}\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right)}$

104850.subject: Physics
104850.text:
An electron in a hydrogen atom has a total energy of $-3.4$ eV. If the magnitude of the centripetal force acting on the electron is approximately $5.1 \times 10^{-9}$ N, the radial distance of the electron from the nucleus is :
(Take $1$ eV $= 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ J)
104850.sol:
The kinetic energy $K$ of an electron is equal to the magnitude of its total energy $E$.
$K = |E| = 3.4 \text{ eV}$

Converting this to Joules:
$K = 3.4 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J} = 5.44 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$

The centripetal force $F_c$ is provided by the electrostatic force, and is related to kinetic energy as:
$F_c = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$

Since $K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, we can write $mv^2 = 2K$.
Substituting this into the force equation gives:
$F_c = \dfrac{2K}{r}$

Rearranging for the radial distance $r$:
$r = \dfrac{2K}{F_c}$

Substituting the given values:
$r = \dfrac{2 \times 5.44 \times 10^{-19}}{5.1 \times 10^{-9}}$

$r = \dfrac{10.88 \times 10^{-19}}{5.1 \times 10^{-9}} \approx 2.13 \times 10^{-10} \text{ m}$

This is approximately $2.1 \times 10^{-10}$ m.

Answer: $2.1 \times 10^{-10}$ m

105001.subject: Physics
105001.text: Two nuclei have mass numbers $27$ and $125$ respectively. What is the ratio of their nuclear radii and the ratio of their nuclear densities?
105001.sol:
The radius of a nucleus is related to its mass number $A$ by the formula $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$.

For the two nuclei with mass numbers $A_1 = 27$ and $A_2 = 125$, the ratio of their radii is:
$\dfrac{R_1}{R_2} = \left(\dfrac{A_1}{A_2}\right)^{1/3} = \left(\dfrac{27}{125}\right)^{1/3} = \dfrac{3}{5}$

Therefore, the ratio of their radii is $3 : 5$.

The nuclear density is approximately constant for all nuclei and is independent of the mass number $A$.

Therefore, the ratio of their nuclear densities is $1 : 1$.

Answer: $3 : 5$ and $1 : 1$

Active nuclei at $t=11$ hour

105234.subject: Physics
105234.text: In which of the following cases is the p-n junction diode reverse biased?
options: p-side is connected to $-5\text{ V}$ and n-side is connected to $-2\text{ V}$
p-side is connected to $+2\text{ V}$ and n-side is connected to $-2\text{ V}$
p-side is connected to $0\text{ V}$ and n-side is connected to $-3\text{ V}$
p-side is connected to $-2\text{ V}$ and n-side is connected to $-5\text{ V}$
105234.sol:
A p-n junction diode is reverse biased when the electric potential at the p-side is lower than the electric potential at the n-side ($V_p < V_n$).

In the first option, $V_p = -5\text{ V}$ and $V_n = -2\text{ V}$. Since $-5\text{ V} < -2\text{ V}$, this diode is reverse biased.

In the second option, $V_p = +2\text{ V}$ and $V_n = -2\text{ V}$ ($+2 > -2$, forward biased).

In the third option, $V_p = 0\text{ V}$ and $V_n = -3\text{ V}$ ($0 > -3$, forward biased).

In the fourth option, $V_p = -2\text{ V}$ and $V_n = -5\text{ V}$ ($-2 > -5$, forward biased).

Answer: p-side is connected to $-5\text{ V}$ and n-side is connected to $-2\text{ V}$

106417.subject: Chemistry
106417.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The maximum number of electrons in a d-subshell is $10$, and its permissible $m_l$ values range from $-2$ to $+2$.
Reason (R): For a given value of azimuthal quantum number $l$, there are $(2l + 1)$ possible values of magnetic quantum number $m_l$, and according to Pauli's exclusion principle, each orbital can accommodate a maximum of two electrons.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
106417.sol:
Evaluate Assertion (A): For a d-subshell, the azimuthal quantum number $l = 2$. The permissible values of the magnetic quantum number $m_l$ range from $-l$ to $+l$, which are $-2, -1, 0, +1, +2$. This gives a total of $5$ orbitals. Since each orbital can hold a maximum of $2$ electrons, the maximum number of electrons in the d-subshell is $5 \times 2 = 10$. Thus, Assertion (A) is true.

Evaluate Reason (R): The formula $(2l + 1)$ correctly gives the total number of orbitals in a subshell for a given $l$. Pauli's exclusion principle states that an orbital can accommodate a maximum of two electrons (with opposite spins). This theoretical basis leads directly to the maximum electron capacity of $2(2l + 1)$ for any subshell. Thus, Reason (R) is true and correctly explains Assertion (A).

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)

106566.subject: Chemistry
106566.text:
Assertion : Nuclear binding energy per nucleon is in the order $-{ }_4^9 \mathrm{Be}>{ }_3^7 \mathrm{Li}>{ }_2^4 \mathrm{He}$.
Reason : Binding energy per nucleon increases linearly with difference in number of neutrons and protons.
options: If both assertion and reason are true and reason is the correct explanation of assertion
If both assertion and reason are true but reason is not the correct explanation of assertion
If assertion is true but reason is false
If both assertion and reason are false.
106566.sol: Binding energy per nucleon of ${ }_3 \mathrm{Li}^7(5.38$ $\mathrm{MeV})$ is lesser than ${ }_2 \mathrm{He}^4(7.08 \mathrm{MeV})$ as helium is found to be more stable than Li. As the atomic mass number increases, the binding energy per nucleon decreases. As the atomic number and the atomic mass number increase, the repulsive electrostatic forces within the nucleus increase due to the greater number of protons in the heavy elements. To overcome this increased repulsion, the proportion of neutrons in the nucleus must increase to maintain stability. This increase in the neutron-to-proton ratio only partially compensates for the growing proton-proton repulsive force in the heavier, naturally occurring elements. Because the repulsive forces are increasing, less energy must be supplied, on the average, to remove a nucleon from the nucleus. The binding energy per nucleon has decreased. The binding energy per nucleon of a nucleus is an indication of its degree of stability. Generally, the more stable nuclides have higher binding energy per nucleon than the less stable ones. The increase in binding energy per nucleon as the atomic mass number decreases from 260 to 60 is the primary reason for the energy liberation in the fission process. The increase in the binding energy per nucleon as the atomic mass number increases from 1 to 60 is the reason for the energy liberation in the fusion process, which is the opposite reaction of fission.

The general trend across a period is an increase in first ionization enthalpy due to increasing effective nuclear charge. However, Nitrogen ($\mathrm{N}$, $2s^2 2p^3$) has a higher first ionization enthalpy than Oxygen ($\mathrm{O}$, $2s^2 2p^4$) because of the extra stability associated with its exactly half-filled $2p$ subshell.

Thus, the correct increasing order of first ionization enthalpy is $\mathrm{B} < \mathrm{C} < \mathrm{O} < \mathrm{N}$.

Arranging the given numerical values in increasing order: $801 < 1086 < 1314 < 1402 \ \mathrm{kJ \ mol^{-1}}$.

Matching the elements to these values:
Boron ($\mathrm{B}$) = $801 \ \mathrm{kJ \ mol^{-1}}$ (IV)
Carbon ($\mathrm{C}$) = $1086 \ \mathrm{kJ \ mol^{-1}}$ (III)
Oxygen ($\mathrm{O}$) = $1314 \ \mathrm{kJ \ mol^{-1}}$ (II)
Nitrogen ($\mathrm{N}$) = $1402 \ \mathrm{kJ \ mol^{-1}}$ (I)

Therefore, the correct match is (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II).

Answer: (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
